stem: A 51-year-old man with a 15 pack-year smoking history is admitted to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset left pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. His BP is 105/70 mmHg, and his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. He has decreased breath sounds on the left-hand side. A chest X-ray reveals a 3-cm left- sided pneumothorax. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Chest drain
This patient is symptomatic from a large (3 cm) pneumothorax and has high-risk features, including a significant smoking history and age greater than 50 years. This necessitates a chest drain as the most appropriate intervention for his pneumothorax. Other features which make up the list of high-risk features to watch out for include significant hypoxia, haemodynamic compromise and haemopneumothorax.

Ambulatory device
Ambulatory devices are considered for pneumothoraces without high-risk features. In this case, the size of the pneumothorax and high-risk features mean that a chest drain is most appropriate.

Conservative management
Conservative management is not appropriate, given the size of the pneumothorax and this patient has high-risk features. It is only appropriate for patients who are asymptomatic with a small pneumothorax.

stem: A 34-year-old woman, who has recently completed a course of treatment for chronic myeloid leukaemia, presents to the Emergency Department with dull ache affecting the right hip, which she says came on all of a sudden. She is unable to walk more than 20 m without severe pain, and flexion and external rotation are severely limited. MRI shows evidence of marrow ischaemia affecting the femoral head. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
Core decompression with bone grafting
Osteonecrosis of the hip is the likely diagnosis here, given the sudden-onset pain and presence of marrow oedema indicating ischaemia. It is progressive in many cases despite intervention, but given the patient's young age, decompression and bone grafting should be attempted. The decompression procedure can stimulate new blood vessel growth and, with inclusion of bone growth factors as part of the surgical procedure, may improve the success of engraftment. Over time, deterioration of symptoms may necessitate a total hip replacement.

Nifedipine
Although osteonecrosis of the femoral head may be related to microvascular disease, there is little evidence to support the use of calcium channel antagonists as medical therapy. Core decompression with bone grafting is the intervention of choice, given this patient's young age.

Osteotomy
Osteotomy is a historical option for treatment of osteonecrosis of the femoral head. It was thought to be useful to offload damaged areas with respect to weight-bearing. It does not significantly impact prognosis and may make total hip replacement more difficult when it is eventually required.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic due to deteriorating kidney function. She complains of multiple joint pains and problems with photosensitivity over the past few months. Her BP is 152/90 mmHg, and her heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 23 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 307 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 135 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Complement C3 10 mg/dl 90–180 mg/dl Urinalysis Blood 1+, protein 2+ What is the most likely cause of this patient's renal impairment?
explanation:
Lupus nephritis
This patient has problems with skin photosensitivity and small joint polyarthritis. There is also evidence of renal vasculitis with abnormal Cr concentration, haematuria and proteinuria. The low C3 concentration suggests that there is ongoing tissue immune complex deposition, which is a strong pointer to lupus nephritis. A renal biopsy is the logical next step to confirm the diagnosis, with immunosuppression as the preferred initial intervention.

stem: An 85-year-old man who is receiving palliative care for metastatic colon cancer is admitted to the Oncology Ward with nausea, vomiting, progressive abdominal distension and colic. His abdomen is markedly distended, with quiet bowel sounds. An NG tube is positioned for symptomatic relief. What is the most appropriate antiemetic to control this patient's nausea and vomiting?
explanation:
Haloperidol
Haloperidol is the intervention of choice for patients with nausea and vomiting who are receiving end-of-life care for bowel obstruction. It is usually given as a stat dose of 2.5 mg subcutaneously, followed by 2.5 mg over a 24-hour period. The dose may be uptitrated to 5 mg over 24 hours. Hyoscine is also given to relieve symptoms of colic, and dexamethasone can have additive effects in reducing nausea.

Domperidone
Domperidone is not recommended for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in end-of-life care where there is bowel obstruction with colic. It has a peripheral stimulant action on GI tract smooth muscle, which can significantly worsen symptoms of colic.

Hyoscine
Hyoscine is a muscle relaxant, which is the intervention of choice to reduce symptoms of colic. It can be given subcutaneously, with a stat dose of 20 mg, followed by 60 mg over 24 hours, usually delivered with a syringe driver. It does not relieve symptoms of nausea, for which haloperidol is a better option.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the Psychiatry Clinic by her husband. He is concerned as she seems to be very keen on washing her hands multiple times per day and refuses to leave the house. Her mother died from MRSA infection following a hip replacement 18 months ago. The patient refuses to sit in a chair, and when asked to do so, she starts to cry and says she believes she will get MRSA. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Mysophobia
Mysophobia is specifically a fear of germs. In this case, it seems the death of her mother due to MRSA has made the patient develop a phobia of catching the disease herself. This is manifested by a refusal to sit down on a chair in the hospital. Cognitive behavioural therapy is the initial intervention of choice to manage mysophobia.

Adjustment disorder
An adjustment disorder is a maladaptive response to a psychological stressor. Patients often feel severe emotional distress, with an increased risk of self-harm ensuing. Although this patient has had an abnormal response to her mother's death from MRSA, it has manifested as a phobia rather than with features of adjustment disorder.

Agoraphobia
Agoraphobia is a fear of leaving locations which an individual knows or considers to be safe. This patient's inability to leave the house might suggest agoraphobia. However, the mention of MRSA confirms that this specific fear of infection is the basis of her symptoms, making mysophobia the likely diagnosis.

stem: A 62-year-old man is reviewed in the Diabetes Clinic. He has hypertension and mild heart failure, and has failed to tolerate metformin due to diarrhoea. His BP is 155/85 mmHg, and his heart rate is 74 bpm and regular. His BMI is 32 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 148 g/l 130–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 302 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 123 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Glycated Hb (HbA1c) 63 mmol/mol Less than 48 mmol/mol What is the most appropriate way to manage this patient's glucose control?
explanation:
Dapagliflozin
This patient has mild heart failure and an elevated Cr concentration against a background of type II diabetes. In this situation, given that he has failed to tolerate metformin, a sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, such as dapagliflozin, is the most appropriate next step, according to guidelines from National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. The SGLT2 inhibitor class has positive effects on renal and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with and those without type II diabetes, reduces blood glucose concentration and has a modest positive impact with respect to weight reduction.

stem: A 70-year-old man attends the Memory Clinic with his wife. She is concerned because he has been misplacing items around the house, waking very early in the morning and then sleeping in the day, and has twice called her from the local shop saying that he is lost. He retired from his job at the family solicitors two years ago, saying that he was finding the pace too fast. Neurological examination is unremarkable. He scores 24/30 on a Mini- Mental State Examination (MMSE). What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Alzheimer's disease
This patient has several features of Alzheimer's disease, including short-term memory loss, episodes of disorientation with respect to place and a disordered sleep pattern. The MMSE score is supportive of the diagnosis. MRI, with or without additional single-photon emission CT, is the gold standard approach to diagnosing the condition. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are the mainstay of therapy.

Depression
Depression could account for sleep disturbance and a degree of forgetfulness, although it is not commonly associated with sudden episodes of deterioration in place. This feature, coupled with the marked reduction in MMSE score, is more suggestive of Alzheimer's disease.

Lewy body disease
Lewy body disease presents with features of dementia and motor signs of Parkinsonism, such as increased tone and cog-wheeling, although tremor is usually much less marked vs Parkinson's disease. Visual hallucinations are a prominent feature of Lewy body disease.

stem: A 53-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for the results of his upper GI endoscopy and biopsy following symptoms of indigestion and small-volume haematemesis. The biopsy shows evidence of gastric MALToma and he is Helicobacter pylori-positive. What is the most appropriate management of this patient?
explanation:
H. pylori eradication therapy
H. pylori eradication therapy is the intervention of choice for patients diagnosed with gastric MALToma, even if they are H. pylori-negative at the point of diagnosis. Studies suggest it promotes resolution in up to 80% of cases of gastric MALToma with early disease. A course of proton pump inhibitor, combined with two antibiotics from a choice of three (clarithromycin, amoxicillin or metronidazole), is the usual regimen.

Gastric radiotherapy
Gastric radiotherapy is the intervention of choice for gastric MALToma where there has been an inadequate response to H. pylori eradication therapy and a rituximab-based chemotherapy regimen.

Imatinib
Imatinib is not part of standard therapy for gastric MALToma. It may be considered for some patients with a systemic disease that is resistant to rituximab-based chemotherapy. It is a standard treatment for chronic myeloid leukaemia.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance. She also complains of excessive snoring and says she can no longer wear her rings due to swollen fingers. Her BP is 155/92 mmHg, and her BMI is 23 kg/m 2. She has macroglossia. What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
Serum insulin-like growth factor 1
Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is produced by the liver and its concentration parallels that of growth hormone. In contrast to growth hormone, however, IGF-1 has a long half-life, which makes it appropriate to measure as a random outpatient sample. It is, therefore, the initial investigation of choice for this patient, who has hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance, macroglossia, peripheral oedema and a normal BMI, all of which fit with acromegaly.

24-hour 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid
The 24-hour 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid (5-HIAA) test is a useful screening test for carcinoid syndrome, which is suggested by episodes of tachycardia, facial flushing and diarrhoea.

24-hour urinary free cortisol
The 24-hour urinary free cortisol test is the investigation of choice for Cushing syndrome, which is suggested by marked weight gain, hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance. This patient's symptoms are more consistent with acromegaly.

stem: Three individuals from the same family, aged 54, 22 and 21 years, present to the Emergency Department. They have been having projectile vomiting for the past hour. A meal of fried rice from a Chinese takeaway was eaten four hours earlier. What is the most likely cause of these patients' symptoms?
explanation:
Bacillus cereus
B. cereus is well known as a contaminant of fried rice, particularly if it is reheated after it has been left standing for a prolonged period. According to the subtype of the bacterium, either an emetic toxin (cereulide) or a diarrhoeal toxin can be produced. Symptoms generally begin within 1–6 hours of ingestion of contaminated rice and resolve without intervention 6–24 hours after ingestion.

Norovirus
Norovirus is associated with projectile vomiting and watery diarrhoea. It would be highly unusual to see three patients presenting with vomiting at the same time. Hence, bacterial contamination of food is much more likely to be the cause of the symptoms seen here.

Salmonella typhi
S. typhi is associated with abdominal pain, diarrhoea and fevers over a more prolonged time period. The symptoms reported here are more consistent with B. cereus contamination of fried rice.

stem: A 47-year-old woman is referred to the Respiratory Clinic for asthma control. She is currently taking fluticasone 500 μg twice daily, salmeterol 50 mg twice daily and montelukast. Despite this, she has required four courses of PO prednisolone in the past year. Her peak expiratory flow rate is 350 litres/min (500 predicted). Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 115 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 12.3 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Eosinophils 3.2 × 10 9/l 0.05–0.5 × 10 9/l Chest X-ray Clear lung fields What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Omalizumab
Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that specifically targets the immunoglobulin E receptor, preventing its interaction with mast cells, eosinophils and basophils. The patient has evidence of allergic asthma with poor control (four courses of PO steroids) and a raised eosinophil count, putting her in the category where Chat by omalizumab is indicated. It is dosed every 2–4 weeks, with the dose determined body weight (between 75 mg and 600 mg).

High-dose prednisolone and itraconazole
Prednisolone and itraconazole are indicated for the treatment of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). In ABPA, there is usually patchy shadowing on the chest X-ray, which is absent here.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with severe headache, double vision and loss of sense of smell. According to her husband, she has been increasingly drowsy and confused over the past 48 hours. A previous DVT led to the identification that she is heterozygous for factor V Leiden. Her temperature is 37.8 °C, and her BP is 165/88 mmHg. She has bilateral optic disc swelling and is unable to comply with basic commands. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Cerebral venous thrombosis
This patient has had a gradual deterioration over a few days, with evidence of cranial nerve palsy (loss of sense of smell), raised intracranial pressure and increased risk of venous thrombosis. This raises the possibility of underlying cerebral venous thrombosis, for which magnetic resonance venography is the investigation of choice. Anticoagulation is the intervention of choice over the longer term.

Herpes simplex encephalitis
Herpes simplex encephalitis has a predilection for the temporal lobes. This leads to progressive deterioration in behaviour, short-term memory loss and drowsiness that builds over a few days. The factor V Leiden heterozygosity is a stronger pointer to cerebral venous thrombosis.

Ischaemic stroke
Ischaemic stroke is associated with sudden deterioration with focal neurological signs. The gradual worsening of symptoms with headache and papilloedema seen here is more likely due to venous thrombosis.

stem: A cardiovascular outcome trial is reported for roxagliptin, a new diabetes therapy added to standard of care vs standard of care alone. A total of 3.5% of patients given the drug were hospitalised for heart failure vs 2.8% of those treated with standard of care alone. The risk appeared to be increased in patients with baseline renal impairment. What is the best way to evaluate the risk of heart failure vs baseline characteristics?
explanation:
Multivariable modelling with backward elimination
Multivariable modelling with backward elimination is the optimal way to determine which baseline characteristics contribute to the risk of heart failure. A constellation of risk factors are identified, and backward elimination then removes those which contribute least to an increased risk. This analysis is what was deployed in the saxagliptin study referenced here.

Prospective cohort study
A prospective cohort study would take many years to accumulate sufficient patient exposure to analyse which baseline characteristics are associated with a risk of heart failure. A multivariable analysis is the most appropriate next step to contribute to prescribing information.

Retrospective cohort study
A retrospective cohort study is not an option here to investigate the risk of a new therapy causing heart failure because it is extremely unlikely that a sufficient number of patient years of exposure would have been accumulated.

stem: A 59-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of recent-onset double vision. He has type II diabetes, and takes metformin and dapagliflozin. He has horizontal diplopia, with failure to adduct the left eye. There is nystagmus affecting the right eye. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia fits with the symptoms here, where there is the failure of adduction of the eye on the affected side and nystagmus on the contralateral side. This is consistent with injury to the medial longitudinal fasciculus, which can occur as a result of a small vessel stroke related to diabetes mellitus or inflammatory conditions such as multiple sclerosis. In most cases, the prognosis is good, with gradual recovery over a period of months.

Abducens nerve palsy
An abducens nerve palsy results in paralysis of the lateral rectus muscle and failure to abduct the eye on the affected side. The combination of failure of adduction with nystagmus affecting the other eye is more consistent with internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Cerebellar stroke
A cerebellar stroke is more likely to lead to bilateral nystagmus and an unstable gait. The differential eye signs seen here are more consistent with internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with a photosensitive rash and multiple small joint polyarthritis. She has also suffered from night sweats and gradual weight loss over the past few months. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be positive in this patient?
explanation:
Antinuclear
This patient's symptoms are typical of systemic lupus erythematosus, with a photosensitive rash and small joint polyarthritis. Ninety-five per cent or more of patients with lupus are positive for antinuclear antibodies. Other antibodies, such as Ro and La, may be found but are not characteristic of the disease.

Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies are associated with rheumatoid arthritis, not with lupus (the likely diagnosis here), where antinuclear antibodies are most commonly found.

Anti-La
Anti-La antibodies are associated with Sjögren syndrome. When present in pregnant women with lupus, they are associated with an increased risk of neonatal heart block and should prompt more Chat aggressive immunosuppression.

Anti-mitochondrial
Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are strongly associated with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) and are found in 95% or more of patients with the disease.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with diarrhoea, weight loss and multiple joint pains. A biopsy shows villous atrophy with periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive macrophages. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Whipple's disease
Whipple's disease presents with features of malabsorption and arthritis, and small bowel infiltration with PAS- positive macrophages is typical of the condition. The macrophages contain intracellular clumps of Tropheryma whipplei, the causative organism. Prolonged antibiotic treatment is required, usually with a course of IV ceftriaxone for 2–4 weeks, followed by PO sulfamethoxazole for 1–2 years.

Behçet's disease
Behçet's disease is associated with uveitis and oral and genital ulceration, as well as with diarrhoea and joint pains in some cases. It does not fit with the PAS-positive macrophages here, which are characteristic of Whipple's disease.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is associated with diarrhoea and malabsorption. However, features such as dermatitis herpetiformis and an itchy rash affecting the buttocks and posterior thighs are absent here. PAS-positive macrophages are also not a feature of coeliac disease.

stem: A 21-year-old woman who works at a nursery is brought to the Emergency Department following a paracetamol overdose. She had taken 50 × 500 mg tablets and left a note to her parents. Her boyfriend found her and called for an ambulance. She has self-harm marks on both wrists. She had a previous paracetamol overdose four years ago and was admitted to the Emergency Department with alcohol intoxication on three previous occasions. What is this patient's strongest risk factor for successful suicide?
explanation:
Previous self-harm
A number of meta-analyses have attempted to rate the risk of suicide mortality according to the characteristics of each case. One such meta-analysis is referenced here. A pooled odds ratio estimate of 10.1 is described for patients who have a previous episode of self-harm. Although some of the other risk factors listed here, such as alcohol use disorder, also impact risk, they are considered lesser contributors.

Age 21
Increasing age is actually a risk factor for suicide mortality. This is because elderly patients are more likely to be socially isolated, may have chronic disease and may suffer financial deprivation, all of which are incremental risk factors.

Alcohol use disorder
Alcohol use disorder carries an odds ratio of 3.2 for suicide mortality. It is thought to be a risk factor for impulsivity. This is less than the potential incremental risk for previous self-harm attempts.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with eye and throat itching, a hives-like rash and shortness of breath after taking her second dose of amoxicillin. She is treated with IM adrenaline, which resolves her symptoms. What is the most useful investigation?
explanation:
Mast cell tryptase
Mast cell tryptase increases with mast cell degranulation and is a key feature of anaphylaxis, the most likely diagnosis here, given the exposure to amoxicillin. Levels peak within 30–90 minutes after the onset of symptoms. The reference range is 2–14 μg/l, and taking a trough level 24 hours after the episode is useful. Treatment of anaphylaxis includes IM adrenaline as the mainstay of therapy.

Basophil count
Mast cell degranulation, rather than increased basophils, is associated with acute anaphylaxis. Increased basophils are associated with autoimmune disease and haematological malignancies.

Eosinophil count
Eosinophils may be elevated above the upper limit of normal (0.5 × 10 9/l) in patients with chronic allergy or those with vasculitis or chronic parasitic infection. They are not useful in evaluating anaphylaxis.

Prolactin
Prolactin does not have any value in evaluating anaphylaxis. Its concentration can be acutely elevated after an epileptic fit, in which case it can help to differentiate between non-epileptic and epileptic seizures.

stem: A 69-year-old man who has advanced Parkinson's disease is reviewed by his General Practitioner. His current medications include co-careldopa, entacapone and ropinirole. His motor symptoms are well controlled, although when his medications are reduced, he experiences disabling off symptoms. His main complaint is of multiple syncopal episodes when he gets up from a chair after meals or gets up too quickly in the morning. He has tried TED stockings, with minor improvement. His lying BP is 142/80 mmHg, which falls to 105/65 mmHg on standing. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Midodrine
Midodrine is an alpha-1 adrenergic agonist considered a first-line intervention for patients with postural hypotension despite non-pharmacological measures such as TED stockings. Dosing is 2.5–10 mg, given up to three times daily. Supine hypertension and urinary retention are adverse effects of concern.

Atomoxetine
Atomoxetine is a noradrenaline reuptake transporter inhibitor licensed for the treatment of attention- deficit/hyperactivity disorder. It can also be used off-licence in the treatment of orthostatic hypotension. However, it is not usually a first-choice option.

Modafinil
Modafinil is a dopamine reuptake inhibitor used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. It may improve alertness in patients with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, although it does not significantly impact postural BP.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department following a collapse at the airport after returning from a holiday to Kenya. She is complaining of left-sided pleuritic chest pain and has a swollen left leg. Her BP is 85/50 mmHg, and her heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. Her chest is clear on auscultation, and her respiratory rate is 38 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation on air is 91%. An ECG and ECHO reveal right ventricular strain. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Alteplase
This patient has a large pulmonary embolism, with haemodynamic instability and evidence of right ventricular strain. She is at imminent risk of cardiorespiratory arrest, and thrombolysis is the only appropriate option. The recommended dose for pulmonary embolism is 0.9 mg/kg delivered over a period of 60 minutes.

Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent, not an anticoagulant or a thrombolytic. As such, it is ineffective in managing pulmonary embolism and should not be used here. Thrombolysis is most appropriate.

Dalteparin
Low-molecular weight heparin, such as dalteparin, is the usual first-line option for pulmonary embolism. In this case, however, with features of haemodynamic instability, the best option is thrombolysis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred to the Neurology Clinic with episodes of sudden, sharp, stabbing pain over her left cheek. The pain can last from a few seconds to up to 30 seconds in duration and may occur many times per day. She says the pain can be triggered by cleaning her teeth or going out in cold weather. Neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate first-line intervention?
explanation:
Carbamazepine
This patient's symptoms are typical of trigeminal neuralgia, and the normal neurological findings in the clinic are in keeping with this diagnosis. Carbamazepine is understood to carry the best evidence for medical therapy, and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends treatment until patients have had no episodes for one month, then attempting to wean off the treatment. Gabapentin and pregabalin are also thought to be effective. For patients who do not respond to therapy, one of the available surgical trigeminal nerve decompression procedures may be appropriate.

Gabapentin
Gabapentin and pregabalin are both potential second-line alternatives for the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia, the diagnosis here, when carbamazepine is unsuitable or ineffective.

Ibuprofen
Although trigeminal neuralgia is thought to be related to compression or entrapment of the trigeminal nerve, NSAIDs are not effective in relieving pain symptoms. Antiepileptics, such as carbamazepine, are the appropriate first-line intervention.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is reviewed on the Haematology Ward 48 hours after beginning induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia. A significant deterioration in her renal function has been noted. Her BP is 90/60 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 87 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 21.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 109 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 6.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 −) 17 mmol/l 22–32 mmol/l Phosphate 1.9 mmol/l 0.8–1.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 395 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l What is the most important abnormality to treat at this stage?
explanation:
Hyperkalaemia
Although this patient has tumour lysis syndrome as a result of hyperuricaemia related to cell lysis, the most urgent problem which requires intervention is hyperkalaemia, which puts the patient at risk of cardiac arrest. The patient should receive cardiac monitoring. In the first instance, a cardioprotective dose of calcium gluconate is given. This should be followed by adequate rehydration and correction of hypotension, insulin and dextrose to reduce the K + concentration acutely and treatment for hyperuricaemia.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is referred to the Oncology Clinic with anaemia and weight loss of 3 kg over the past month. She has developed hyperpigmentation of both axillae, with skin thickening, and has a papillomatous lesion in the mouth. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 92 g/l 120–160 g/l Which of the following cancers is most likely to be the cause of this patient's skin changes?
explanation:
Gastric carcinoma
Acanthosis nigricans is most commonly associated with syndromes of insulin resistance, obesity and type II diabetes. It has also been described in association with malignancy, most commonly gastric cancer, which could account for the anaemia and weight loss seen here. An increase in transforming growth factor is thought to be responsible. In total, around 60% of malignant cases are thought to be due to gastric cancer.

Breast cancer
Acanthosis nigricans, the diagnosis here, is described in association with breast cancer, although the association is much less strong than for gastric carcinoma. Symptoms resolve with treatment of the underlying tumour.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is not associated with acanthosis nigricans. Skin metastases are common and are seen as red/blue nodules, which are usually painless.

stem: A 72-year-old man is commenced on atorvastatin 80 mg following a myocardial infarction. What is the mode of action of atorvastatin?
options: Inhibitor of Niemann–Pick C1-like 1/cholesterol complex endocytosis
explanation:
3-hydroxy-3-methyl-coenzyme A reductase inhibitor
Statins function as inhibitors of 3-hydroxy-3-methyl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase. This blocks the rate- limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis and reduces plasma cholesterol concentrations. They can be combined with other agents, including fibrates, bempadoic acid, ezetimibe and PSCK9 inhibitors. Many are metabolised by CYP3A4, so care should be exercised when co-prescribing them with potent P450 inhibitors.

Adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase activator
Metformin is an indirect adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase activator. It reduces glucose concentration, has modest positive effects on body weight and improves the lipid profile, with positive effects on high-density lipoprotein and triglyceride concentrations.

Adenosine triphosphate citrate lyase inhibitor
Bempadoic acid is an adenosine triphosphate citrate lyase inhibitor. It blocks the biosynthesis of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Therefore, it has additive effects on reducing LDL cholesterol concentration, in addition to statin therapy.

Inhibitor of Niemann–Pick C1-like 1/cholesterol complex endocytosis
Ezetimibe is an inhibitor of Niemann–Pick C1-like 1/cholesterol complex endocytosis. It reduces cholesterol absorption from the small bowel and can be used in combination with other agents such as statins.

stem: A 20-year-old rough sleeper is admitted to the Emergency Department with fever, cough and confusion over the past 36 hours. He has been seen three times over the past 12 months with alcohol intoxication. His temperature is 38.6 °C, his BP is 95/60 mmHg, and his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. There are coarse crackles at the right base on auscultation of the chest. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 130–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 13.4 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 75 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 195 mg/l Less than 10 mg/l Sodium (Na +) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Chest X-ray Right lower lobe consolidation with cavity formation What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Klebsiella pneumonia
Patients with a history of alcoholism and malnutrition are at much higher risk of Klebsiella respiratory tract infection. This leads to consolidation, with areas of cavitation and lung abscess formation, as seen here. Klebsiella is sensitive to treatment with cephalosporins, quinolones and carbapenems, which can be used in monotherapy.

stem: A 77-year-old woman who has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and left ventricular failure presents to the Emergency Department with coryzal symptoms, a dry cough, fevers and muscle aches. Her temperature is 39 °C; her BP is 105/82 mmHg, and her heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. There are coarse crackles at the left base on auscultation. Saturation is 91% on air. What is the most important next investigation to confirm diagnosis?
options: Throat swab for respiratory virus PCR
explanation:
Throat swab for respiratory virus PCR
Given the coryzal symptoms and muscle aches, a throat swab PCR for respiratory virus informs where and how this patient should be treated and any additional therapies that could be introduced, apart from antibiotics, such as antiviral therapy for coronavirus disease 2019 infection. As such, it is important to process the sample with point-of-care testing as early as possible.

Arterial blood gases
This patient's oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry is measured at 91%, which may well be in the normal range for her, given her history of COPD. At this stage, with respect to infection control risk, screening for respiratory viruses, including severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus 2 and respiratory syncytial virus, is most important.

Blood cultures
Blood cultures may identify a potential cause of pneumonia, but sputum culture is likely to have a higher yield. In any case, empirical antibiotic treatment with co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin should be commenced for community-acquired pneumonia.

stem: A 22-year-old man visits the Genetics Clinic with his partner. He has been diagnosed with Fabry's disease, but his partner is unaffected. They want to start a family. What is the chance of their son being affected by the condition?
explanation:
0%
Fabry's disease is an X-linked condition, meaning that affected men carry one affected X chromosome and one Y chromosome. For this reason, all of their sons will be unaffected by the disorder and all of their daughters will have Fabry's disease. Penetrance of Fabry's disease in women is 70% or more, with symptoms generally milder than in men.

25%
A 25% risk is the risk of the offspring of two carriers of an autosomal recessive disease producing an affected child. In this case, Fabry's disease is X-linked, meaning that all daughters of the man who is affected will inherit the disease, but no son will.

50%
Women with Fabry's disease have a 50% chance of passing on their affected X chromosome to any offspring, irrespective of gender. Men can only pass on their affected X chromosome to their daughters.

75%
A 75% risk of passing on an affected gene does not fit with the X-linked inheritance pattern of Fabry's disease. Given the man is affected here, only daughters will be affected by Fabry's disease.

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by the police. He told them he is the son of god and had been trying to break the windows of the local store because the devil is broadcasting through the television. He has also tried to slit his wrists because voices are telling him to kill himself. He has covered his room in tinfoil because he is concerned the devil is transmitting messages to his brain. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Schizophrenia
This patient has significant delusions, believing that he is the son of god and the devil is transmitting messages into his brain via the television. He appears to have no insight into his illness, consistent with an underlying diagnosis of schizophrenia. An atypical antipsychotic agent, such as risperidone, is the initial intervention of choice.

Bipolar disorder
Delusions, including an individual believing they are the son of god, are seen during manic periods associated with bipolar disorder. The voices encouraging suicide and the delusions around thought insertion are much more consistent with schizophrenia.

Drug-induced psychosis
Drug-induced psychosis is a possible diagnosis here, although there are no indication given here of drug abuse. The delusions of thought insertion are highly suggestive of a diagnosis of schizophrenia.

stem: A 74-year-old man who smokes 10 cigarettes per day is admitted to the Emergency Department with a cough and chronic confusion. According to his son, he has become increasingly tired and confused over the past three weeks. His BP is 123/60 mmHg, and his heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. On auscultation of the chest, he has a wheeze consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Investigation Value Normal range Haemoglobin (Hb) 110 g/l 130–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.9 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 302 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 118 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 93 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Chest X-ray Left hilar mass What is the most appropriate way to treat this patient's hyponatraemia?
explanation:
Fluid restriction
This patient has a hilar mass, which may be due to an underlying small cell lung cancer against a background of smoking. Small cell lung cancers are recognised to produce antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which likely accounts for the confusion and hyponatraemia seen here. In the first instance, fluid restriction is appropriate, although additional demeclocycline may be required to induce renal diabetes inspidus. Treatment of the underlying cancer can reduce ADH production and improve symptoms. A volume of 1200 ml per 24 hours is a usual starting point for target restriction of fluids.

stem: A 64-year-old man is reviewed on the Respiratory Ward five days after the insertion of a chest drain for a large spontaneous pneumothorax. He has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) treated with dual inhaled therapy. The chest drain is continuing to bubble. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Video-assisted thoracoscopic pleurodesis
Video-assisted thoracoscopic repair of this persistent air leak is the intervention of choice, given this patient's history of COPD and the high risk of a medical procedure such as blood patching and failing to seal the hole. Other procedures such as talc pleurodesis are usually reserved for malignant effusion. Blood patching is an option if the patient refuses or is unable to undergo surgery.

Blood patch pleurodesis
Blood patch pleurodesis is usually considered for patients with a persistent air leak related to pneumothorax who are unable or unwilling to undergo surgery. This patient's COPD puts him at high risk of recurrence, meaning that video-assisted thoracoscopic repair as the definitive procedure is preferred

Clamping the drain
Clamping the drain is not recommended for any patient with a drain inserted for a pneumothorax. The fact that it is still bubbling implies a persistent air leak, and clamping may actually increase the size of the pneumothorax again.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is referred to the Haematology Clinic after an episode of prolonged bleeding following the extraction of two wisdom teeth. She also reports that her periods have always been heavy. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 112 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 229 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Prothrombin time (PT) 13 seconds 12.3–15.1 seconds Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 50 seconds 29–43 seconds What is the most likely cause of this patient's bleeding symptoms?
explanation:
Von Willebrand's disease
Von Willebrand's disease is subject to autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive inheritance and leads to an increased risk of bleeding. Up to 50% of patients with von Willebrand's disease have prolonged APTT. Although some women who carry the haemophilia genes may have slightly prolonged APTT, this does not usually lead to clinically significant disease. The prolonged APTT seen in von Willebrand's disease occurs due to low levels of factor VIII because von Willebrand factor protects factor VIII from degradation. Desmopressin is the treatment of choice for patients with type 1 von Willebrand's disease because it causes a rise in both von Willebrand factor and factor VIII concentration within 30–60 minutes, meaning that it can be used just before minor surgical procedures.

stem: An 18-year-old man who lives in assisted living accommodation is admitted to the Emergency Department with status epilepticus. His seizure activity appears predominantly left-sided, and he has a port-wine stain affecting the right side of the forehead and upper eyelid. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Sturge–Weber syndrome
Sturge–Weber syndrome is associated with a port-wine stain, which is unilateral and affects the upper face, and epilepsy where seizure activity is seen on the opposite side. Seizures occur due to the development of leptomeningeal angiomas, which affect the surface of the brain and become calcified over time. Progressive cognitive impairment is also seen.

Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is associated with the development of multiple cutaneous neurofibromas. Café-au-lait spots and axillary freckling are also seen. Intracerebral neurofibromas can lead to intellectual impairment and seizures.

Neurofibromatosis type 2
Neurofibromatosis type 2 is associated with the development of vestibular schwannomas. These present with hearing loss, tinnitus and balance disorders, with symptoms beginning in teenage years.

stem: A 54-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic. He is having difficulty with swallowing and walking, and has problems with fine movements of his hands, which are interfering with his job as an electrician. There are mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs, with increased tone and weakness of the arm extensors, and decreased tone with bilateral foot drop on examination of the legs. No sensory loss is present. What is the most useful investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Electromyography
This patient has mixed upper and lower motor neurone dysfunction, with intact sensation. Given the absence of other features, this marks out motor neurone disease (MND) as the most likely cause of his symptoms, for which electromyography is the most useful investigation. Electromyography reveals polyphasic motor units, with the presence of fibrillation and fasciculations. The greatest innovation with respect to treatment in recent years has been the recognition of the value of non-invasive ventilation in managing fatigue.

Autoantibody screen
Autoantibodies may be useful in ruling out inflammatory myositis. However, in the first instance, electromyography is most useful in looking for the typical features of MND, the likely diagnosis here.

Lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture is not useful in diagnosing MND, for which electromyography is the intervention of choice. However, it may be of value in investigating other causes of limb weakness such as Guillain–Barre syndrome and multiple sclerosis.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with fever, muscle rigidity, drowsiness and confusion. She is treated with long-term lithium for bipolar disorder and has recently been prescribed tramadol for a back injury. Her temperature is 39 °C, and her BP is 155/90 mmHg; her pupils are dilated. Muscle tone is increased; there is hyperreflexia, with spontaneous clonus. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
options: Impaired serotonin reuptake into the presynaptic neurone
explanation:
Impaired serotonin reuptake into the presynaptic neurone
When tramadol and lithium are used together, this drives a reduction in the reuptake of serotonin from the synaptic cleft into the presynaptic neurone. This leads to symptoms of serotonin syndrome, the diagnosis here, with pyrexia, hypertension, dilated pupils and increased muscle activity. Tramadol should be withdrawn immediately. Benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine, a mixed histamine receptor antagonist, are potential interventions.

D2 dopamine receptor antagonism
The presentation here fits better with serotonin syndrome rather than with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). NMS is related to D2 antagonism and leads to similar symptoms to those of serotonin syndrome, but does not occur in relation to tramadol and lithium co-prescription.

Increased serotonin release
Increased serotonin release as a cause of serotonin syndrome, the diagnosis here, occurs as a result of the use of amphetamines and their derivatives, such as MDMA, and as a result of mirtazapine, which is an antidepressant.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is referred to the Dermatology Clinic for umbilicated lesions that have appeared over the past few months. They affect the line of her waistband and her buttocks in particular. She says that when she scratches the lesions, they occasionally leave a scar. She has no underlying medical illnesses and plays hockey in a local team. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Molluscum contagiosum
Molluscum contagiosum leads to crops of umbilicated lesions, often found around the inner thighs or genital region. It is caused by a pox virus, which may be spread by fomites such as towels or shared sports gear. Most cases clear without intervention after around 18 months, although autoinoculation can lead to the appearance of more lesions. Patients should be encouraged to avoid scratching because of scarring and the risk of infection.

Bacterial folliculitis
Folliculitis is characterised by inflammation around hair follicles, which is usually bacterial in origin. Small erythematous papules may be seen next to the follicle. Topical antibacterial wash can lead to resolution of symptoms.

Human herpesvirus 6 infection
Human herpesvirus 6 causes a childhood illness known as roseola infantum. It causes coryzal symptoms, fever and an erythematous rash, but it does not cause the umbilicated lesions seen here.

stem: A 65-year-old man is assessed in the Oncology Clinic following a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus. He has a hoarse voice, and a paralysed right vocal cord is noted. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 99 g/l 130–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 11.0 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 267 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Calcium 2.86 mmol/l 2.1–2.65 mmol/l Chest X-ray Right upper lobe cancer Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) 1.7 litres Which feature is the most important contraindication against pneumonectomy?
explanation:
Vocal cord palsy
Vocal cord palsy is the most important contraindication against pneumonectomy. This is because it implies local invasion, meaning that pneumonectomy would not convey a survival advantage and is likely to be associated with significant operative morbidity. In place of surgery, this patient should be offered access to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

stem: A 43-year-old woman who has systemic lupus erythematosus presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She says that although her joint pains are controlled on hydroxychloroquine, she is feeling increasingly tired over the past few months. Her BP is 149/89 mmHg, and her heart rate is 83 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 22 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 100 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 207 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Urinalysis Blood 1+, protein 2+ What is the best way to manage this patient's lupus?
explanation:
Switch hydroxychloroquine to mycophenolate mofetil
Hydroxychloroquine is the intervention of choice for joint disease associated with lupus. However, for patients with active renal disease, as is likely here, mycophenolate mofetil is preferred. The usual starting dose of mycophenolate mofetil is 500 mg twice daily for the first week. It is increased to 1 g twice daily from week two. For patients with highly active lupus, prednisolone may be used in combination.

stem: A 57-year-old man is admitted to the Cardiology Ward with a new-onset murmur and fever. Blood culture results are positive for Streptococcus bovis. An ECHO confirms the diagnosis. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Colonoscopy
S. bovis endocarditis, the most likely diagnosis here, is most strongly associated with colon cancer. Case series suggest between 25% and 80% of cases are associated with an underlying colorectal tumour. This makes a colonoscopy the most useful next investigation. In patients whose investigation of the colon is unremarkable, the biliary tract should be investigated next, as S. bovis may also be associated with biliary tract infection and cirrhotic bacteraemia.

Abdominal ultrasound
S. bovis endocarditis is most associated with colon cancer. The pickup rate for colon cancer with abdominal ultrasound is very poor, meaning that a colonoscopy, rather than ultrasound, is the preferred next step.

Dental examination
Streptococcus viridans, rather than S. bovis, is associated with dental infection as a cause of endocarditis. In this case, a colonoscopy is the most appropriate next investigation.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset left eye pain and severe left- sided headache. He says that symptoms began with blurred vision a few hours earlier, and his acuity is now reduced to counting fingers only. The globe feels hard to touch, and there is ciliary flush. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Angle-closure glaucoma
The rapid deterioration in vision, coupled with ciliary flush and a hard globe, fits best with an episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Intraocular pressure should be measured, and a pressure of above 21 mmHg is confirmatory. IV acetazolamide is used acutely, and topical therapies include beta blockers, corticosteroids and pilocarpine. After a single uncomplicated episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma, the prognosis is usually considered excellent.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion presents with sudden-onset painless unilateral visual loss. In essence, it is a ‘stroke of the eye’. The pain and increased globe pressure would be unusual for a retinal artery occlusion.

Keratitis
Keratitis is associated with blurred vision, a red and painful eye and a sensation of a foreign body. It is not associated with the hard globe seen here, which is suggestive of acute closed-angle glaucoma.

stem: A 54-year-old woman, who has rheumatoid arthritis, is admitted to the Emergency Department 48 hours after receiving an intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the right knee. She has a temperature of 38.6 °C; the knee is swollen and red, and flexion is limited to 30 degrees. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Septic arthritis
Septic arthritis is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms, given the very recent corticosteroid injection into the knee. Aspiration for microscopy, culture and sensitivity is the next step. Antibiotics should be started before results are available, with flucloxacillin as the default option, given the likelihood of staphylococcal infection. In the event that septic arthritis is confirmed, then washout should be considered.

Acute gout
A first flare of acute gout would be unusual, given this patient has a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis and had a recent knee injection. Septic arthritis is much more likely and can be confirmed by aspiration.

Pre-patellar bursitis
Pre-patellar bursitis, also known as housemaid's knee, can be precipitated by repeated kneeling. Because of this, it is common among professionals such as carpet fitters. The symptoms are in the wrong site for this to be housemaid's knee.

stem: A 42-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with Hashimoto's disease is commenced on levothyroxine replacement therapy. Which of the following is a short-term physiological response to levothyroxine in a hypothyroid patient?
explanation:
Increased osteoclast activity
Bone mineral density is often increased in patients with hypothyroidism, and bone turnover with remodelling is reduced. Once thyroxine replacement is commenced, there is an increase in both osteoblast and osteoclast activity, although the biggest increase is in osteoclast activity.

Decreased calcitonin concentration
Hypothyroidism is associated with decreased concentrations of calcitonin. Supplementation of calcitonin via intranasal delivery has been shown to impact quality of life.

Decreased osteoblast activity
Bone turnover is increased in response to commencement of thyroxine replacement. Levels of osteoblast and osteoclast activity increase, although a larger rise in activity is seen for osteoclast activity, which is associated with a slight reduction in bone mineral density.

Decreased hydroxylated vitamin D concentration
Hypothyroidism is associated with a reduction in 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration in many patients. Supplementation of vitamin D, as well as of thyroxine, has been shown in some studies to improve patient wellbeing. Thyroxine alone does not significantly impact vitamin D concentrations.

stem: You are investigating the cause of a lysosomal storage disorder that leads to progressive neurological dysfunction, muscle weakness and cardiac failure. What is the function of lysosomes?
explanation:
Protein degradation
Lysosomes are responsible for the degradation of macromolecules, including intracellular proteins. They are particularly important for breaking down and recycling of malfunctioning organelles and, in some cases, can drive apoptosis in cases where a cell is irreversibly damaged.

DNA replication
DNA replication is primarily driven by DNA polymerase, which catalyses the joining of deoxyribonucleoside 5'- triphosphates to form the growing DNA chain. Lysosomes are responsible for protein breakdown.

DNA transcription
DNA transcription occurs in the nucleus, and DNA is transcribed by RNA polymerase. Translation, whereby a peptide is formed by using the RNA template, occurs in the cytoplasm. Lysosomes are responsible for breaking down macromolecules in the cell.

Post-translational protein modification
Post-translational modification of lipid molecules takes place in the Golgi body. Lysosomes are responsible for breaking down intracellular components, including proteins.

stem: A 54-year-old man is managed on the Coronary Care Unit following an inferior myocardial infarction. He suffers a witnessed ventricular tachycardia (VT) arrest and is given a 150-J shock. The ECG still shows VT, and he does not have a palpable pulse. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Deliver another shock at 150 Joules
In cases of witnessed and monitored cardiac arrest due to VF/VT where immediate defibrillation can be performed, delivering up to three quick successive shocks before starting CPR is recommended by some advanced life support guidelines.

Adrenaline
Administering adrenaline is important during advanced cardiac life support, especially if VF/pulseless VT persists despite initial shocks and good-quality CPR cycles every few minutes; however, it is not indicated immediately following an unsuccessful first defibrillation attempt in this scenario.

Commence CPR
Commencing immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) after an unsuccessful defibrillation attempt aligns with standard ALS protocols for unwitnessed arrests or when VF/pulseless VT persists after multiple shocks; however, since this was a witnessed arrest with immediate monitoring, further shocks are prioritized.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with confusion and a dry cough of 1-week duration. His BP is 132/82 mmHg, and he has crackles at the left base on the auscultation of the chest. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/l 130–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 13.1 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 88 mg/l Less than 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 191 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 116 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 97 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Urea 7 mmol/l 2.5–7.8 mmol/l Glucose 5 mmol/l Less than 7 mmol/l What is this patient's calculated osmolarity?

253
This patient's calculated osmolarity is 253 mOsm/l. It is calculated by adding together twice the Na + concentration in mmol/l, twice the K + concentration and the glucose and urea concentrations.
